newsitem.title: CANADA: Buba's Hartmann - Gold plan threat to credible euro.
newsitem.headline: Buba's Hartmann - Gold plan threat to credible euro.

text.p: Controversial plans by the German government to revalue central bank assets could undermine the credibility of Europe's planned currency union, Bundesbank directorate member Wendelin Hartmann said on Friday.

"This action could ... undermine the credibility of EMU by creating a one-off measure without solving the basic budgetary problems of Germany," Hartmann told a conference at the Forex 97 meeting in Toronto.

German Finance Minister Theo Waigel put forward a plan to revalue German currency and gold reserves now, using some of the proceeds to shore up Germany's finances in order to qualify for Europe's currency union.

Hartmann reiterated the Bundesbank's statement, which said that the proposal would interfere with Bundesbank independence in its mandate of responsibility for money supply and monetary policy and compromise Germany's position in the runup to currency union.

Hartmann said that he did not think that market foreign exchange rates on the final day before the launch of the euro single currency in 1999 would be used as final conversion rate for the new currency.
"In my view, it is not very likely that the market rates on the very last day before the start of EMU will be taken as a basis (for conversion rates)," Hartmann said.
No date has yet been set for when a value will be put on the fledgling currency.
Hartmann also insisted that he was against any postponement of Europe's planned single currency.

"I personally think that postponement is not a good idea," Hartmann said, adding that by postponement he meant a delay of one or two years, not a delay of one or two months because of parliamentary hold-ups.
He also said that if any delay to EMU were planned, the decision should be made early in order to prevent wasted efforts.

Asked whether the Bundesbank would stimulate the economy to help Germany qualify for EMU, Hartmann said that the Bundesbank was not responsible for economic growth in Germany and that it had done all it could to help facilitate growth.
"What we can do is done. We have done our duty in this context," Hartmann said.
"The constraints of economic growth are different, they do not lie in the financial environment, they do not lie in the interest rate field, which is the influential area of the Bundesbank," he said.
